lead: Diathermy means heating deep tissue on purpose without cutting the skin. A short-wave unit passes a radio-frequency current through the body at 27.12 MHz. A microwave unit beams 2450 MHz energy into tissue. An ultrasonic unit sends 0.8–1 MHz sound waves through a coupling gel. The tissue absorbs the energy and becomes warm. This relieves pain, relaxes muscle spasm and speeds repair in physiotherapy. Surgical diathermy uses the same radio-frequency idea to cut and coagulate, but that is a separate application, not therapy.
prereq: You need: basic AC circuits — frequency f in hertz, wavelength λ = c ÷ f with c the speed of light, and impedance — plus the idea that current needs a complete path.

blocks.text: A short-wave diathermy unit takes 50 Hz mains, rectifies it, and feeds an oscillator. The oscillator runs at 27.12 MHz. A power amplifier raises the signal to a useful output, commonly up to about 200 W (watts). A matching network tunes the amplifier to the patient, because the body is not a fixed 50 ohm load. The output then reaches the applicator: two insulated plates, or a coil. In capacitive coupling the plates sit on either side of the limb, so the tissue between them is the dielectric (the material between the plates) and it heats. In inductive coupling a coil is placed near the body and its changing magnetic field induces small circulating currents, called eddy currents. Some units allow both.

Tissue heats by two losses. Dielectric loss: the alternating electric field makes polar water molecules rotate. Their collisions with neighbours turn field energy into heat. Resistive loss: ions in tissue drift with the field and collide. Both depend on frequency and on tissue composition. Muscle has more water and ions than fat, so it usually absorbs more short-wave energy.

Penetration falls as frequency rises. The 27.12 MHz wave is about 11 m in air, far longer than the body, so the field passes through the body rather than being blocked at the skin. This gives deep heating. 27.12 MHz is a reserved industrial–scientific–medical frequency, not any random short-wave radio channel. 13.56 MHz is also used.

Microwave diathermy uses 2450 MHz. A microwave oscillator, such as a magnetron, feeds a reflector applicator. The applicator directs a beam into the tissue, and the water in tissue absorbs it. The wavelength in air is about 12.2 cm, but tissue absorbs strongly, so useful heating is only a few centimetres deep. Keep the applicator at the stated distance. Do not treat over the eye or testis, where little tissue protects the organ. Microwaves are convenient for superficial joints and muscles.

Ultrasonic diathermy uses a piezoelectric transducer (a crystal that vibrates when driven by a voltage) at 0.8–1 MHz. The transducer converts electrical drive into mechanical vibration. A coupling gel removes air, because air reflects ultrasound. The beam enters tissue and is absorbed; the patient feels warmth. 1 MHz reaches several centimetres. 3 MHz is used for more superficial tissue. Bone and air interfaces absorb or reflect strongly, so avoid directing the beam across a bone edge or through air.

All three methods raise tissue temperature. The dose is set by output power in watts and time in minutes. The operator starts low and asks the patient about warmth and pain. Skin sensation is the safety sensor; if it is impaired, the patient cannot warn of a burn.

Dose is not just a number on the dial. It is power in watts applied for a time in minutes, and it depends on the applicator, the body part and the patient's sensation. A physiotherapy session may last 10–20 minutes, but the setting is adjusted to a comfortable warmth. Burns can occur at high power, with poor coupling, with wrinkled towels or with a metal implant that concentrates the field.

Contraindications include metal implants in the field, pregnancy over the abdomen or pelvis, ischaemic tissue (poor blood supply), bleeding tissue and impaired sensation. A cardiac pacemaker or other electronic implant is also a reason to avoid short-wave and microwave diathermy, because the field can interfere with the device. Do not treat over the eye, testis or growing bone with microwave or ultrasound unless specifically trained.

Surgical diathermy, or electrosurgery, uses radio-frequency current for cutting and coagulation (clotting). A small active electrode creates high current density, so tissue vaporises and the cut seals small vessels. A large return plate spreads the current. It is not therapy and not the same as heating a joint. The same RF principle appears in cardiac ablation, where a catheter burns a small patch of heart muscle; see 5.9.

examples.question: A short-wave diathermy unit works at 27.12 MHz. Find the wavelength in air and the period of the wave.
steps: Given f = 27.12 MHz = 27.12 × 10⁶ Hz and c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s.
The 11 m wavelength is far bigger than the body, so the field passes through tissue rather than being blocked by it.
examples.answer: Wavelength λ = 11.06 m and period T = 36.9 ns.

traps: Higher frequency always means deeper heating. It is the opposite for electromagnetic diathermy: 2450 MHz microwaves heat only a few centimetres, while 27.12 MHz short waves heat deeper.
27.12 MHz is any convenient short-wave radio band. It is a reserved industrial–scientific–medical frequency; 13.56 MHz is another.
Diathermy and surgical diathermy are the same. Therapeutic diathermy warms tissue; electrosurgery cuts and coagulates with concentrated RF current.
Dose is set by power alone. Dose is power in watts times time in minutes, and it also depends on coupling, applicator and the patient's sensation.
Ultrasound at 3 MHz penetrates deeper than 1 MHz. Absorption rises with frequency, so 3 MHz heats more superficially.

quiz.q: State the standard frequency and two applicator arrangements for short-wave diathermy.
quiz.a: 27.12 MHz; insulated capacitive plates or an inductive coil.
Metal implants in the field and pregnancy over the abdomen or pelvis; also ischaemic or bleeding tissue.

quiz.q: Why is a matching network needed between the amplifier and the applicator plates?
quiz.a: The patient's impedance changes with body part and coupling. The network tunes the output to that impedance, so power transfers efficiently and the amplifier is not damaged by a mismatch.

quiz.q: Why does muscle usually heat more than fat in short-wave diathermy?
quiz.a: Muscle has more water and ions, so both dielectric loss and resistive loss are larger. Fat has less polar water and lower conductivity, so it absorbs less.

quiz.q: A microwave diathermy unit runs at 2450 MHz. Find the wavelength in air.
A short-wave unit delivers 200 W for 10 minutes. Find the energy in joules.
Why does 1 MHz ultrasound reach deeper than 3 MHz ultrasound?
quiz.a: Absorption rises with frequency. At 3 MHz, the energy is absorbed in the first centimetres, so less reaches deep tissue. At 1 MHz, absorption per centimetre is lower, so the beam penetrates further.

quiz.q: A patient with a hip implant needs deep heating of the thigh. Why is short-wave diathermy risky, and what should be done?
quiz.a: Metal concentrates the electric field and can cause a local burn; the implant may also be near the return path. Avoid short-wave or microwave over the implant, or choose a method and field that keep the implant out of the heated volume, following local safety rules.

beyond: Not for the exam. Microwave ablation and radio-frequency ablation now destroy tumours and faulty heart tissue using the same heating idea, with imaging guidance. High-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) uses focused ultrasound to heat a small volume while sparing skin. Wearable and phased-array applicators are research areas for controlled deep heating. Search terms: microwave ablation, RF ablation, HIFU, specific absorption rate (SAR), diathermy safety.
